newsitem.title: USA: Clinton recovering "very well" from surgery.
newsitem.headline: Clinton recovering "very well" from surgery.

text.p: President Bill Clinton was described as doing "very well" on Saturday as he recovered from surgery to repair a torn tendon and began limited therapy with the aid of the surgeon who operated on him.
Clinton, recovering at Bethesda National Naval Medical Centre in suburban Maryland, ate breakfast and was in an upbeat mood, according to those in contact with him.
"He's doing very well ... He's in excellent spirits," said Dr. David Adkinson, the surgeon who performed the operation on Friday and examined his patient on Saturday.

Adkinson said Clinton rested comfortably overnight and was "focused" on recovering. The physican, based at the naval facility, said Clinton began an early and limited therapy programme -- typical for all patients who have undergone such a procedure.
Adkinson said he slowly moved the president's right knee up and down several times -- a process that will be repeated several times daily during the early stages of Clinton's recovery.
Dr. Daniel Sewell, who assisted in the operation and also visited with Clinton on Saturday, also offered a positive assessment. "He's doing great. We're very happy."
Vice President Al Gore, who substituted for Clinton in delivering the president's weekly radio address to the nation, said at the start of the address that "the president's doing great."
"He's resting comfortable and he'll be back on his feet, both of them, very soon," said Gore.
Clinton caught his heel on a step at the Florida estate of Australian golfer Greg Norman early on Friday, tearing the quadriceps tendon connecting the kneecap to the upper thigh in his right leg.
The knee-buckling tumble will put Clinton on crutches for about eight weeks and the president's doctors said it was likely to be six months before he could return to his regular running and golf.
White House officials, however, remained upbeat that Clinton would be able to go ahead with plans to meet in Helsinki on Wednesday with Russian President Boris Yeltsin.
The accident has forced the postponement of a planned White House visit by Jordan's King Hussein that had been set for Tuesday.
A senior State Department official said another possible diplomatic casualty of the president's accident could be a scheduled Monday meeting with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov.

The surgery also led to a delay in a two-week trip to Africa planned by first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton. She delayed her planned Saturday departure until Sunday to ensure that her husband was alright, aides said.
